summary: This government bill is a new Maldives Immigration Act that would replace the Immigration Act (Law No. 1/2007) and the Maldives Passport Act (Law No. 79/78). It sets up Maldives Immigration as its own civil service outside the Maldives Civil Service, led by a Controller General appointed by the President. It sets the rules for entering and leaving the country, passenger and biometric data, Maldivian passports, six types of visa for foreigners, inspections, and the return, detention and deportation of foreigners who have no right to be in the country. The scans are hard to read in places, especially the articles on who is barred from entry and on inspections, so some details are uncertain.
whyItMatters: Every traveller would have biometric data taken at the border, and airlines and ship operators would have to send passenger and crew lists to Immigration in advance. Foreigners could be held in an immigration detention centre for up to 12 months while awaiting deportation, with regular reviews and the option of bail.
keyProvisions: Article 5 creates Maldives Immigration as a separate civil service outside the Maldives Civil Service and moves over the staff, property and legal duties of the current Maldives Immigration under the home affairs ministry. The minister sets immigration policy (Article 3).

Articles 8 and 10 say the President appoints the Controller General on the minister's advice for a 4-year term, renewable once. The person must be a Maldivian citizen, not a citizen of another country, and not yet 55, and can be removed for reasons such as losing the qualifications or misconduct. Officers act with legal protection for things done in good faith (Article 17) and can serve until age 65 (Article 22).

Article 25 says every Maldivian has the right to leave, enter and stay in the Maldives without a permit and can never be deported. Articles 27, 29 and 30 require entry and exit only through approved ports, with fines of up to MVR 50,000 for false declarations, MVR 100,000 for using unapproved ports and up to MVR 200,000 for a vessel operator who refuses to take a person back on board.

Article 31 lets Immigration collect biometric data from everyone arriving and leaving, with a privacy impact assessment in consultation with the Privacy Commissioner. Under Article 32, vessel and airline operators must share passenger and crew details in advance, and this data may be kept for no more than 48 hours except in special cases. Article 33 allows an electronic travel authorisation for citizens of countries the minister names.

Articles 36 to 43 set out ordinary, diplomatic and official passports, biometric passports, cancelling and holding passports, reporting lost passports and temporary travel documents. Article 46 lists foreigners who cannot be allowed in, including security risks, people wanted by the International Criminal Court or Interpol, people with certain public health risks, and holders of Israeli passports. Article 48 and Schedule 1 create visitor, family, work, business/investor, study and special-purpose visas, each with subtypes such as tourist, spouse, domestic worker and research visas.

Articles 59 to 66 let the Controller General send back people refused entry and deport foreigners who break the law, either for a set period or permanently. A person cannot be deported to a country where they face a risk to life or torture (Article 61). Detention is capped at 12 months, must be reviewed every 28 days, goes to the Civil Court for review after 4 months, and people can be released on bail. Detainees must be told the reason in writing in a language they understand, get access to a lawyer and their consulate, and see a doctor within 24 hours. The law would take effect 3 months after it is published in the Government Gazette (Article 72).
whoIsAffected: All travellers entering or leaving the Maldives, foreign workers, visitors, investors and students, airlines and ship operators, Maldivians applying for passports, and immigration staff.
statedReasons: The government says the bill sets up Maldives Immigration as a separate civil service and sets the rules for entering and leaving the Maldives, issuing passports to Maldivians, permits for foreigners to come and stay, and dealing with people who have no permit to enter or stay.
